L1861@P42: Abstract : Here we present an adapted version of the Modified Gaussian Model (MGM), a tool developed to detect and
L1862@P42: characterize both simple and complex mineralogies in magmatic rocks, and we review the results we obtained over the last years
L1863@P42: on four different planetary bodies.
L1864@P42: We first describe the working principle of the adapted MGM technique, with the differences compared to the original version,
L1865@P42: and the validation process using various laboratory and natural spectra. We then describe the results obtained on the Oman ophiolite
L1866@P42: (Earth), taken as a planetary spectral analog for magmatic terrains. We finally present spectroscopy-based mineralogical maps and some
L1867@P42: petrologic implications for key regions of Mars, the Moon and asteroid Vesta.

L1878@P43: Abstract : The ChemCam instrument package on the Mars rover, “Curiosity”, is the first planetary instrument that
L1879@P43: employs laser- induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) to determine the compositions of geological samples on another planet.
L1880@P43: However, the sampled spectra are often corrupted by various sources of interferences that would largely affect the accuracy of
L1881@P43: elemental concentration estimation. Therefore, pre- processing is essential to improve the quality of the spectra. This paper revisits
L1882@P43: the conventional preprocessing procedures where denoising is followed by continuum removal. Through comprehensive performance evaluation, we propose a new procedure that would lead to much improved estimation accuracy. First, we show that the
L1883@P43: denoising process should be conducted after continuum removal. Second, a state-of-the- art image denoising technique is adapted
L1884@P43: to the 1D domain to boost the performance of denoising. Third, an additional preprocessing step is added that effectively select
L1885@P43: the most informative spectral bands. All these approaches have largely improved the accuracy of concentration estimation with
L1886@P43: band selection being the most effective.

L1891@P43: Abstract : CRISM (Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars) hyperspectral data have a spatial resolution ranging from 12 to 36m/pixel allowing the high resolution mapping of minerals at the surface of Mars. However, the
L1892@P43: signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) makes challenging the discrimination of minerals spectrally close such as certain phyllosilicates and
L1893@P43: carbonates. Here, we discuss different processing of data reduction used to improve the signal-to-noise ratio and to highlight the
L1894@P43: alteration minerals at the surface of Mars and their limit. We show that our tool allows to understand trends in global mineralogy
L1895@P43: present in hyperspectral data cube.

L1902@P43: Abstract : In this study, we test the ability of neural networks to determine the composition of magmatic rocks from
L1903@P43: their laboratory spectra. We first describe the structure and behaviour of the multilayer perceptron that we implement and train
L1904@P43: for quantitative characterization. For that purpose, reference laboratory spectra of mafic minerals from both natural and synthetic
L1905@P43: samples are used. As their composition in terms of the three mafic minerals, olivine (OL), orthopyroxene (OPX) and clinopyroxene (CPX) are known, those spectra are given as inputs during the learning phase of the neural network. In the analysis phase,
L1906@P43: we use the neural network to process spectra acquired on SNCs (Shergottites, Nakhlites, Chassignites) meteorite samples that are
L1907@P43: considered to be representative of Mars surface. The network outputs mineralogical compositions very quickly, performing only
L1908@P43: explicit operations. Our preliminary results show that neural networks are able to quantify mafic minerals, especially in the case
L1909@P43: of complex mixtures, with much improved computer efficiency and comparable accuracy compared to usual methods. This is very
L1910@P43: promising regarding future analysis of huge datasets.

L1920@P44: Abstract : For optically complex waters, the optical classification was suggested to be a good solution to improve the
L1921@P44: retrieval of biogeochemical products, and more appropriate for large-scale complex waters than classical regional waters. Around
L1922@P44: China there are turbid lakes, complex rivers and highly contrasted coastal regions, so the study provided an applicable classification strategy for characterizing the optical variability of the optically complex waters of Chaohu Lake, Three Gorges, Dianchi Lake,
L1923@P44: Taihu Lake, and Huanghe estuary waters. An improved K-means algorithm based on spectral angle distance was used to cluster an
L1924@P44: in situ data set of remote sensing reflectance spectra (447 stations) into five optical classes. The combination of the characteristic
L1925@P44: wavelengths, a set of features of spectra to distinguish the waters into five optical types was provided. This work provides an effective set of features of spectra to divide the optically complex waters around China and the potential of class-specific inversion
L1926@P44: methods for deriving bio-optical products by the satellite images in optically complex waters.

L1931@P44: Abstract : In this paper, we suggest optimal flat fields for calibration of hyperspectral data (EO1) - predominantly of
L1932@P44: urban nature. We compare the suitability of various flat field candidates by performing vegetation, soil, and impervious surface
L1933@P44: (VIS) classification. Flat Field methods provide 90% average overall accuracy (with best 100% and 77% worst accuracies) over
L1934@P44: number of conducted experiments. Flat fields show marginal improvement over IAR. Most common urban land covers such as
L1935@P44: play grounds, concrete parking lots, and especially industrial roof covers have been found adequate for the image calibration.

L1940@P44: Abstract : To promote cross-calibration or information extraction involving hyperspectral reflectance data from different sources, a method for restoring reflectance of a higher spectral resolution from hyperspectral radiance data is proposed. It
L1941@P44: involves three steps: spectral super-resolution of radiance data, transformation to the higher resolution of interest, and radiativetransfer-model-based atmospheric correction. The spectral resolution of the super-resolved radiance and the spectral response
L1942@P44: model of the restored reflectance were analyzed. The restored reflectance matches the library spectrum better than the directly
L1943@P44: inversed and the interpolated reflectance spectra in the validation experiment based on HyMap data and USGS spectral library.
L1944@P44: This method is theoretically applicable to get reflectance of a relative lower spectral resolution as well.

L1956@P45: Abstract : The control of thickness homogeneity is a major concern in steel industry for quality issues. In the case of oil,
L1957@P45: an inhomogeneous coating on whole strip surface can create oxidation and lubrication trouble during coiling. Nowadays, different
L1958@P45: commercial solutions exist on the market (Light induced fluorescence, infrared gauges) but mainly for punctual measurements.
L1959@P45: The ability of new devices to characterize thin oil layers have been studied in this paper. This poster is focused on the study of
L1960@P45: spatial homogeneity for oil layer detection on steel surface for potential new online solution. The results presented in this paper
L1961@P45: confirm the interest of devices working in 3-5 μm spectral range to potentially answer to industrial needs.

L1965@P45: Abstract : The Havemann-Taylor Fast Radiative Transfer Code (HT- FRTC) is based on Principal Components (PCs)
L1966@P45: and allows fast and exact radiance and/or transmittance calculations. It is ideally suited for the simulation of hyperspectral sensors with hundreds or thousands of channels. The HT-FRTC can simulate a full instrument spectrum for any atmosphere and
L1967@P45: surface within a few milliseconds. It works for satellite- based, airborne and ground-based sensors. The code has been applied in
L1968@P45: any part of the spectrum from the short-wave to the long-wave (i.e. infrared plus microwave). It includes the solar and the lunar
L1969@P45: source and can account for the spherical Earth. The HT-FRTC has been incorporated into a one- dimensional variational (1DVar) retrieval system that also works solely in PC space. This keeps the dimensions of the matrices involved small. The solution of
L1970@P45: the full non-linear problem is achieved by an iterative Levenberg-Marquardt minimization procedure. The retrieval state vector
L1971@P45: includes the vertical profiles of atmospheric temperature, water vapour and ozone, and possibly other trace gases as well as the
L1972@P45: surface temperature and surface emissivity / reflectivity (the latter being represented by a set of PCs). For a scattering atmosphere,
L1973@P45: cloud parameters and aerosol parameters have been added to the state vector. The cloud part of the state vector for cirrus cloud
L1974@P45: includes cloud-top pressure, ice water content, cloud fraction and cloud geometrical thickness. For water cloud there is also an
L1975@P45: effective droplet size.

L1983@P45: Abstract : In this study two neural networks were implemented in order to emulate a retrieval model and to estimate the
L1984@P45: sulphur dioxide (SO2) columnar content and plume height from volcanic eruption. ANNs were trained using all IASI channels in
L1985@P45: TIR as inputs, and the corresponding values of SO2 content and height of plume obtained using the Oxford SO2 retrievals as target
L1986@P45: outputs. The retrieval is demonstrated for the eruption of the Eyjafjallajökull volcano (Iceland) occured in 2010 and to three IASI
L1987@P45: images of the Grímsvötn volcanic eruption that occurred in May 2011, in order to evaluate the networks for a different eruption.
L1988@P45: The results of validation, both for Eyjafjallajökull and Grímsvötn independent datasets, provided RMSE values between neural
L1989@P45: network outputs and targets lower than 20 DU for SO2 total column and 200 mb for plume height, therefore demonstrating the
L1990@P45: feasibility to estimate SO2 values using a neural network approach, and its importance in near real time monitoring activities, owing to its fast application. Concerning the validation carried out with neural networks on images from the Grímsvötn eruption,
L1991@P45: the RMSE of the outputs remained lower than the Standard Deviation (STD) of targets, and the neural network underestimated
L1992@P45: retrieval only where target outputs showed different statistics than those used during the training phase.

L2003@P46: Abstract : X-ray diffraction is a powerful technique to provide information on the molecular structure of samples. Energy dispersive X-ray diffraction (EDXRD) spectra are classically measured at one single fixed scattering angle using a polychromatic X- ray source and a spectroscopic detector. In order to remove system blurring and restore material proper information,
L2004@P46: inversion of the EDXRD spectra is required. This paper proposes to combine EDXRD spectra at different scattering angles to
L2005@P46: improve reconstruction results. To quantify the improvements, detective quantum efficiency (DQE) calculations are used, which
L2006@P46: allow to compare the performance of mono- and multi-angle systems, are used. We present a reconstruction method based on
L2007@P46: multi-angle EDXRD spectra. The algorithm was tested on simulated salt (NaCl) spectra. Finally, advantages of multi-angle over
L2008@P46: mono-angle spectra are discussed.

L2026@P46: Abstract : The physical basis of rock identification is spectral feature. In order to remove the rock spectrum noise, the
L2027@P46: discrete wavelet transform (DWT) was used to deal with the spectra of 13 rock samples of metamorphic rocks collected in mineral
L2028@P46: reservation region. The Biorthogonal 4.4 wavelet of the scale of decomposition was selected was selected as the mother wavelet
L2029@P46: to smooth the spectra and highlight features of absorption. By correspondence analyzing (CA) spectra normalized by DWT, we
L2030@P46: find that the rock spectra were classified into three clusters through analyzing two-dimensional image of CA. The first cluster has
L2031@P46: higher reflectivity than other two clusters, because the compound of light-colored minerals, the key to high reflectivity, of the first
L2032@P46: cluster is greater than that that of other two clusters. The second cluster has obvious iron alteration. The third cluster has obvious
L2033@P46: clay alteration. The results of classification, verified by cluster analysis, are better corresponding. The paper provides a physical
L2034@P46: basis for Metamorphic rocks classification and identification by using remote sensing technology.

L2043@P47: Abstract : The hyperspectral remote sensing in the thermal infrared region is being acknowledged as an innovative tool
L2044@P47: for Earth environmental studies and is complimentary to the optical range. The current study focuses on surface mineral content
L2045@P47: mapping using day and night airborne data in the LWIR spectral range over a well known mineralogical site in Israel. The data
L2046@P47: was acquired with the AisaOWL hyperspectral sensor over Ramon crater in the Negev desert in southern Israel. The identification
L2047@P47: of major minerals was enabled by locating similarities in day and night at-sensor radiance spectra. The analysis resulted with the
L2048@P47: classification of quartz, carbonates, gypsum, kaolinite and other silicates according to their observed spectral features in both day
L2049@P47: and night data.

L2053@P47: Abstract : The present research is developed in the frame of the R&D project GMES4Mining, which aims to support
L2054@P47: particular tasks within the different phases of a mining life cycle [1]. During the exploitation and after the closure of the mine,
L2055@P47: environmental and civil impacts may happen, due to changes in the compacting properties of the soil related to mining activities.
L2056@P47: In this paper, we focus in the emergence of flooded areas, due to a subsidence of the ground surface. Above-ground vegetation
L2057@P47: is affected by changes in groundwater’s dynamics; at first trees suffer defoliation and senescence, and after some time, they die.
L2058@P47: Several methods have been tested, to detect changes in spectral response of forests in a mine area, which are related to imminent
L2059@P47: flooding. ENVI’s Target Detection Tool has been used to estimate the reflectance proportion at pixel level of four targets of interest
L2060@P47: in AISA-Eagle’s data, which are present in flooded areas: water, dead trunks, senescent trees and green stands within water. Five
L2061@P47: target detection’s methods have been tested: Constrained Energy Minimization (CEM), Adaptative Coherence Estimator (ACE),
L2062@P47: Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM), Target-Constrained Interference- Minimized Filter (TCIMF) and Mixture Tuned Matched Filtering (MTMF).
L2063@P47: POSSIBILITIES FOR THE STUDY OF THE NLTE EFFECT ON ATMOSPHERIC CO2 SPECTRAL SIGNATURES INDUCED BY A BLUE JET USING AN INFRARED SPECTRO- IMAGER EMBEDDED IN A STRATOSPHERIC BALLOON.

L2066@P47: F. Duruisseau, N. Huret, Laboratoire de Physique et Chimie de l’Environnement, CNRS and Université d’Orléans, Orléans, France
L2067@P47: Abstract : HALESIS (High Altitude Luminous Events Studied by Infrared Spectro-imagery) is an innovative project
L2068@P47: based on hyperspectral imagery. The purpose of this experience is to measure the atmospheric perturbation in the minutes following the occurrence of Transient Luminous Events (TLEs) from a stratospheric balloon in the altitude range of 20 to 40 km. The
L2069@P47: first part of the study has been dedicated to establish the project feasibility. To do that, we have simulated spectral perturbations
L2070@P47: induced by an isolated blue jet. Simulations have been performed using the line by line radiative transfer model LBLRM taking
L2071@P47: into account the Non Local Thermodynamic Equilibrium. The case of the estimation of the CO2 infrared signature that could be
L2072@P47: the result of a single blue jet occurrence is presented.
L2073@P47: Then, the estimated spectral signatures have been confronted with the technical capabilities of different kinds of hyperspectral imagers. The study has demonstrated the feasibility of the project, but it has also pointed to the challenges to build
L2074@P47: perfectly adapted instrument.

L2093@P48: Abstract : To acquire accurate, real-time hyperspectral images with high spatial resolution, we develop two types of lowcost, lightweight Whisk broom hyperspectral sensors that can be loaded onto lightweight unmanned autonomous vehicle (UAV)
